title: Sel and the Seeds of Courage
markdown:
The wind tore at the tattered banners of a city already bruised by tempest. Salt and shattered glass hung in the air. The Great Unraveling had hammered rain for weeks and smashed greenhouses across the Rooftop District. Below, in his father’s dusty workshop, Sel the glassblower’s apprentice felt a tremor that was not thunder. His hands were steady at the glory-hole. He could spin molten glass into swirling forms. Heights turned those same hands to trembling butter. His stomach churned. His vision blurred. Focus shattered like thin ware.

Rowan was already surveying the damage from her sky-high sanctuary of wilting herbs. She had a way with plants that bordered on magic, fingers as green as the spring leaves she adored, spirit as tough as hardy thyme. Her voice came strong against the gale.

“Sel. The Whispering Gardens. We have to go. Now. The seeds will be gone by morning if Grit finds them first.”

Grit. A scavenger whose eyes glinted with greed, always picking through ruin for profit. The sun was rising. Fail, and the district faced a barren winter.

The Whispering Gardens meant the highest, most precarious greenhouses, perched on the edge of the world, swaying like dandelion fluff. Sel’s throat went dry.

“Rowan, I can’t. You know how I am with heights.”

“You have to.” Firm, kind. “You’re the only one who can shape delicate things. These seeds are like tiny jewels. Incredibly fragile. I can’t carry them all alone, and I certainly can’t climb like you can when you’re not looking down.” Her eyes, usually full of sunshine, held a rare urgency.

They pushed through debris that crunched like brittle ice. Glass shards glittered like fallen stars on ruined pathways. The wind, a mischievous bully, tried to pluck them from the rooftops, tugging cloaks, whipping hair. Rowan led, feet sure, balance uncanny as she navigated the treacherous terrain. Sel followed with white knuckles on every railing, every pipe, every beam that looked as if it might hold. His gaze stayed on her retreating back. The air was damp, thick with the musty scent of decay and the faint sweet promise of hidden life, a confusing mix that mirrored the knot in his stomach. A plank flexed under his heel. He did not look down. He looked at Rowan, and at the pebbles he did not yet hold.

The Whispering Gardens were a chaotic mess. Shattered panes dripped. Pots lay broken. Soil spilled like secrets, tangled roots exposed. Rowan pointed with a dirt-stained finger.

“There. The Bloom-Halls. Sunpetal and Moon-dew. The most important ones.”

The entrance was a gaping maw: a rotten ladder that swayed with every gust. Sel’s breath hitched. His hands went clammy. Then he saw Grit, a greasy shadow slinking in the distance, hunched, avaricious.

“Well, well,” Grit rasped, rust on tin. “Little pretty birds. Come to play in the ruins?”

Sel froze. The old urge: scrabble back to blessedly low ground. He began to turn. Grit wheezed a laugh. “Afraid, little bird?”

Rowan did not scold. She looked at him with a trust that made his heart ache. “These seeds are our future. Think of the first sprouts. The first bloom. The people counting on us.” She opened her palm on tiny smooth pebbles, worn by the sea. “These are for courage. Hold them tight. They remember the strength of the ocean.”

He looked at the pebbles, cool and solid in his palm. Then at Rowan. Not the terrifying drop, the swirling abyss, but the potential for life, the promise of a new season. He took a breath, and another, forced air into his lungs, and started to climb. Rungs groaned a mournful protest. Wind shrieked. He kept his gaze fixed upwards on her encouraging smile and did not look down. Grit watched, a sneer twisting grimy features. A flicker of defiance, small but determined, ignited in Sel’s chest. He reached the top, arms aching with the strain, heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. He was there.

Inside, the air was thick with ancient earth and slumbering life. Rowan darted to a dusty corner. “Sunpetal! Moon-dew! Oh, Sel, we did it!” Grit was already scrambling up, grubby fingers greedy for the pouches.

“Mine!” he snarled.

Sel reacted without thinking. Adrenaline overrode the height. He grabbed a discarded glass bell jar, still miraculously intact, and swung it not to hurt but to ring. A clear sweet chime, a pure note against Grit’s roar. Grit flinched. In that moment Sel scooped the seed pouches into his satchel. Rowan shoved a teetering pile of empty terracotta. Pots tumbled, a chaotic cascade. Grit went sprawling, tangled in pots and roots, more embarrassed than hurt. “You meddling kids!” he sputtered.

They did not wait. They scrambled down faster, seeds clutched against Sel’s chest. The sun began to paint the sky rose and gold.

Later, on Rowan’s rooftop, the wind a gentle whisper, Sel looked out over the city. The greenhouses below were a patchwork of ruin, skeletal remains against the brightening sky. He felt the smooth pebbles in his pocket, a reminder of the ocean’s strength. He took a breath. He did not flinch. He looked down to the streets far below, a dizzying distance, and felt a lightness he had not known. Quiet confidence bloomed. He walked to the edge of the rooftop—a place that once made his stomach twist—and stood there, looking out at the vast expanse. The seeds were saved. So was something else, quieter, and his.
characters: Sel (a glassblower's apprentice), Rowan (a rooftop gardener)
